reasons: Commercial reuse is allowed: NYC Open Data terms only disclaim warranty and liability, the dataset carries no extra agency terms, and the Open Data Law (Admin Code 23-502(d)) says public datasets come with no registration, license or limits on use; cite DOHMH dataset 43nn-pn8j and the pull date.

No field names a private person: the 31 columns are business, inspection, violation, grade and geography fields; a sole proprietor's DBA could be a personal name, so store business fields only and keep the list out of the public repo.
The source is live: rows updated 2026-10-22, daily and automated, latest inspection 2026-10-20, 295,422 rows.

Rows are sustained or not yet adjudicated violations and may hold errors: label each as a cited violation subject to appeal, carry the Legal README notice, never call a restaurant infested or failed; no NYC or NYS rule found barring marketing use (NYS requires a DEC registration for firms advertising pesticide services).
Constitution 2: any public page naming a business with a failed record is major and goes to Todd; names stay inside the paid file and the cold email names no restaurant.

As a small NYC rodent operator I would try $49 a month: about 900 distinct restaurants a month are cited under 04K, 04L, 04M, 04N and 08A with phone numbers on every row, so one won account repays a year.
Free city tools look up one restaurant at a time with no violation or date filter, and pulling pest codes from NYC Open Data takes a query a 3-truck operator will not write.

Competitor prices check out: RatRadar Territory Leads $299 a month per metro, Apify scrapemint $10 per 1,000 rows with no pest filter, so $49 sits in an open gap, though RatRadar adds 311 data and repeat-offender scoring.
The Chicago twin has zero payers, the closest real test of this offer; the reviewer saw $0.00 on its Gumroad page.

Seller-side risk caps the score: the 597-firm roster has no contact fields, 08A is a structural condition not a live infestation, and most cited restaurants already have a pest vendor, so the pitch is a switch pitch.
The same product with the same buyer and motion is live for Chicago at $39 with 0 payers from 57 emails and its outreach is paused; a second city tests the city, not the product.
597 firms are real but hard to reach: the DEC roster has no email, phone or website and many are sole proprietors; the firms with sales staff already buy RatRadar at $299.
A pest citation rarely means a vendor switch: most restaurants already have a pest contract and call it.
